cells.speakerNotes: Welcome everyone. Introduce yourself, the Bay Area Python Interest Group, and the goal: show how marimo combines ordinary Python, reactive execution, and interactive presentation.
Preview the route: compare the notebook models, demonstrate reactivity and widgets, explore data and apps, then close with editor workflow and resources. Invite questions throughout.
Start with the title and the promise of the talk. Marimo is a reactive Python notebook that can also run experiments, query data, and become an app.
Set expectations for a live talk: some slides are rendered directly by marimo, and some moments will switch to a working notebook or app. The code is the presentation.
Use the marimo name as a quick hook. Mari means ball and mo means algae; marimo are spherical algae from Lake Akan. Keep this brief, then connect the idea of a living sphere to a living notebook.
Point out that this deck is built with marimo itself. The useful distinction from conventional slide software is not animation; it is that widgets and Python code remain live during the presentation.

Pause here to open the Jupyter comparison notebook. Tell the audience what to watch for: execution order, saved outputs, and the difference between a static result and a reactive dependency graph. Resume this deck after the demo.
Introduce the people behind marimo: Vincent Warmerdam, Akshay Agrawal, and Sarah Tsai. Correct spelling is Berkeley. Emphasize the project's strong PyData and developer-education roots.

Show that marimo includes a substantial set of native interactive widgets, and mention that custom widgets can be built with Python and anywidget. The improvement to the original note is to name the practical takeaway: start native, extend only when needed.

Transition from the overview into the first hands-on interaction. Ask the audience to notice that the control is a normal Python value in a downstream cell, not a callback that must be wired manually.
Explain the core loop: a cell creates a UI element, another cell reads its value, and dependent output updates automatically. This is the smallest useful example of marimo reactivity.

Many marimo demos begin with a slider, so use this one as the audience's first interaction. Move it through several values and let the dog preference land as a small personal aside without taking over the demo.
Call attention to the dependency chain behind the slider: the slider value determines the cat and dog counts, and the rendered output depends on those counts. No explicit event handler is required.
Introduce the next three widgets: radio selection, multiselect, and checkbox. Ask the audience to predict how each value will appear in Python before interacting with them.
Reinforce the widget lesson: marimo gives the notebook a predictable dataflow graph, so controls, computations, and output stay connected as the user explores.
Transition to the file format. The important claim is that a marimo notebook is Python source, which makes it readable, executable, and straightforward to review in version control.
Explain that the notebook contains no magical second language. Cells parse Python, and the generated file can be formatted, imported, or run as a script with default widget values.
Use the dataframe section to shift from small controls to a real data workflow. Preview filtering, pagination, column selection, transformations, export, and built-in visualization.
Show the multiplication table as a compact example of mo.ui.table. Point out sorting and inspection, then connect the table to the larger California counties example.

Introduce the California county dataset and explain the preparation: clean types, construct zero-padded FIPS identifiers, and calculate population, density, and area ranks before collecting the Polars dataframe.
This cell creates the metric selector and the county dataframe. Explain that the selector is an input to the visualization cell, while the dataframe is shared by the table and charts.

Introduce mo.state as the small piece of shared state that carries a selected county from a Plotly event into the chart description. This avoids hidden mutable state while still supporting interaction.
Switch between Population, Population Density, and Area. Hover for values, then click a county bar. The chart event flows back through Python and updates the selected-county information.
Show the underlying dataframe briefly so the audience can connect the source data to the rendered charts. The same prepared data supports multiple views without duplicating transformations.
Introduce the notebook-to-app idea: the same source can be edited as a notebook, run as an app with code hidden, or deployed. The next view is the interactive county application.
Point out the event-handling cell: selected Plotly points update mo.state. This is a useful example of reactive state crossing a visualization boundary without a custom callback framework.
Introduce the quadratic analyzer as a larger example. It separates inputs, calculations, derived geometry, and rendering while keeping the whole display interactive.
Explain the small q_annotate_point helper. Encapsulating repeated Plotly annotation logic keeps the rendering cell readable and demonstrates that normal Python functions fit naturally in marimo.
Change a, b, and c one at a time. These number widgets are the model inputs; everything else in the analyzer is derived from them.
Show the first derived layer: read widget values and determine whether a is legal for a parabola. Keep the distinction clear between the UI objects and their ordinary numeric values.
Explain that the input controls are composed separately from the calculations. This separation makes the dependency graph easy to inspect and gives the rendering cell clean values to consume.
Use the discriminant to classify the equation as having zero, one, or two real roots. Change inputs to cross those cases and let the audience see downstream cells react.
Show the root calculation for the linear, tangent, and two-root cases. The printed result is intentionally plain Python output, which helps connect the math to the notebook execution model.
Turn on Grid, Vertex, Focus, Directrix, Roots, and Scale XY selectively. These controls demonstrate that one plot can expose several independent reactive options.
Explain the vertex and focus formulas and note that invalid a values are handled explicitly. This is a good moment to show that validation and domain rules belong in ordinary Python.

Describe how the plotted x and y values are derived from the current coefficients and how the range is chosen around the focus and vertex. The plot is data generated by upstream cells, not a static image.
Show the directrix calculation, then enable the Directrix control. Together with the focus and vertex controls, this makes the geometric relationships visible rather than merely stated.

Let the audience drive the analyzer. Change coefficients, toggle annotations, and compare scaled versus unscaled axes. The key takeaway is that a fairly rich app still consists of ordinary Python cells with explicit dependencies.
Transition from application examples to the command line. The goal is to give attendees a few commands they can use immediately after the talk.

Cover marimo edit for creating or editing notebooks, marimo run for serving an app, and marimo convert for bringing in a Jupyter notebook. Keep the command examples visible while explaining the difference between edit and run.
Mention the built-in tutorials, especially dataflow, ui, plots, and for-jupyter-users. These are the fastest next steps for practicing the concepts from the demo.

Introduce editor workflow tips: lazy execution for expensive or side-effecting cells, dependency-aware execution order, and the ability to organize cells for readability rather than execution sequence.

Close the editor section with naming and scope rules. Global names must be unique for reactivity; encapsulate logic in functions or modules, and use underscore-prefixed names for cell-private helpers.

Use the tips accordion as a resource slide rather than reading every item. Highlight save, run stale cells, command palette, formatting, and shutdown; invite attendees to browse the remaining tips later.
This blank transition gives the audience a breath before the resource links. Use it to take final questions or ask what workflow they would most like to try.
Show Molab as a low-friction way to explore marimo in the browser. Explain that attendees can use it to try examples without setting up a local environment first.
Point attendees to the GitHub repository for this presentation. Mention that the slides, source, layout, assets, and comparison notebook are available for inspection and reuse.
